smt-2024-power-01.title: Unpack the definition
smt-2024-power-01.body:
$x\sim y$ means $x\succeq y$ and $y\succeq x$. Swapping the order of the two statements gives $y\succeq x$ and $x\succeq y$, which is exactly $y\sim x$. So indifference is symmetric.

**Answer: Yes**

smt-2024-power-02.title: Induction on the size of $G$
smt-2024-power-02.body: If $|G|=1$, $G=\{x\}$ and $x\succeq x$ (everything is weakly preferred to itself), so $x$ is maximal. Suppose the claim holds for sets of size $n$ and let $|G|=n+1$. Pick any $y\in G$. By the inductive hypothesis $G\setminus\{y\}$ has a maximal element $g$. By completeness, $g\succeq y$ or $y\succeq g$. If $g\succeq y$, then $g$ is maximal in $G$. If $y\succeq g$, then for every $z\in G\setminus\{y\}$ we have $g\succeq z$ and so $y\succeq z$ by transitivity, and $y\succeq y$; so $y$ is maximal in $G$. ∎

smt-2024-power-02.title: Contradiction
smt-2024-power-02.body:
Suppose no maximal element exists. Start with any $x_1$. Since $x_1$ is not maximal, there is $y$ with $x_1
ot\succeq y$; by completeness $y\succeq x_1$. Call it $x_2$ (so $x_2\succeq x_1$ and $x_1
ot\succeq x_2$). Continue: $x_{n+1}\succeq x_n$ while $x_n
ot\succeq x_{n+1}$. Since $G$ is finite, $x_m=x_n$ for some $m>n$. By transitivity, $x_n=x_m\succeq x_{n+1}$ (as $x_m\succeq x_{m-1}\succeq\cdots\succeq x_{n+1}$), contradicting $x_n
ot\succeq x_{n+1}$. ∎

smt-2024-power-03.title: Example
smt-2024-power-03.body:
Let $G=\mathbb Z$ and $x\succeq y$ iff $x\ge y$. It is complete and transitive, but for any integer $n$ we have $n\not\succeq n+1$, so there is no maximal element. (Any valid example works.)

**Answer: $\ge$ on $\mathbb Z$**

smt-2024-power-04.title: Proof
smt-2024-power-04.body:
Let $a\succ b$ and $b\succ c$. Then $a\succeq b$ and $b\succeq c$, so $a\succeq c$ by transitivity of $\succeq$. To show $a\succ c$ it remains to show $c
ot\succeq a$. Suppose instead $c\succeq a$. Then $c\succeq a$ and $a\succeq b$ give $c\succeq b$ by transitivity. But $b\succ c$ means $c
ot\succeq b$, a contradiction. So $c
ot\succeq a$ and $a\succ c$. ∎

smt-2024-power-05.title: Count ordered pairs
smt-2024-power-05.body:
The most weak preferences occur when everything is weakly preferred to everything else, including itself. Each of the $n$ elements can be weakly preferred to each of the $n$ elements, giving $n^2$ ordered pairs.

**Answer: $n^2$**

smt-2024-power-06.title: Use properties of $\ge$
smt-2024-power-06.body: *Complete:* for $a,b\in G$, $u(a)$ and $u(b)$ are real numbers, so $u(a)\ge u(b)$ or $u(b)\ge u(a)$, i.e. $a\succeq b$ or $b\succeq a$. *Transitive:* if $a\succeq b$ and $b\succeq c$ then $u(a)\ge u(b)$ and $u(b)\ge u(c)$, so $u(a)\ge u(c)$, i.e. $a\succeq c$. ∎

smt-2024-power-07.title: Monotonic means order-preserving in both directions
smt-2024-power-07.body: We have $a\succeq b\iff g(a)\ge g(b)$. If $g(a)\ge g(b)$ then either they are equal (so $f(g(a))=f(g(b))$) or $g(a)>g(b)$, giving $f(g(a))>f(g(b))$; in both cases $f(g(a))\ge f(g(b))$. Conversely, if $g(a)<g(b)$ then $f(g(a))<f(g(b))$, so $f(g(a))\ge f(g(b))$ forces $g(a)\ge g(b)$. Hence $a\succeq b\iff (f\circ g)(a)\ge(f\circ g)(b)$. ∎

smt-2024-power-08.title: Find a cycle
smt-2024-power-08.body: $x\succ y$ for society since Alice and Bob prefer $x$ to $y$ (Carl the reverse). $y\succ z$ since Alice and Carl prefer $y$ to $z$. If society's preferences were transitive we would get $x\succ z$; but $z\succ x$ since Bob and Carl prefer $z$ to $x$ (only Alice prefers $x$). So transitivity fails. ∎

smt-2024-power-09.title: Add an irrelevant outcome
smt-2024-power-09.body: Use the same three individuals but add a fourth outcome $I$ ranked last by all: Alice: $x\succ y\succ z\succ I$; Bob: $z\succ x\succ y\succ I$; Carl: $y\succ z\succ x\succ I$. As before, Alice and Bob prefer $x$ to $y$ (so $y$ is not a Condorcet winner), Alice and Carl prefer $y$ to $z$ ($z$ is not), Bob and Carl prefer $z$ to $x$ ($x$ is not), and $I$ loses to every other outcome unanimously. So there is no Condorcet winner. (Any valid example works.)

smt-2024-power-10.title: Walk until a repeat
smt-2024-power-10.body: Since there is no Condorcet winner, for every outcome $x$ there is an outcome $y$ that is preferred to $x$ by at least as many individuals as the other way around; with no ties this means strictly more individuals prefer $y$ to $x$ (we say $y$ *beats* $x$). Start at any outcome $a_0$, let $a_1$ beat $a_0$, $a_2$ beat $a_1$, and so on. Since the set is finite, some outcome repeats: $a_j=a_m$ with $j<m$ and all intermediate outcomes distinct. Reading the loop $a_m,a_{m-1},\dots,a_{j+1}$ backwards from the repeat, each outcome is preferred by more individuals to the previous one in the walk. Relabeling the cycle gives $a_1,\dots,a_n$ with more people preferring $a_i$ to $a_{i+1}$ and more preferring $a_n$ to $a_1$. ∎

smt-2024-power-11.title: Compare distances
smt-2024-power-11.body:
A writer with ideal $b^*$ prefers $7$ to $18$ iff $|b^*-7|<|b^*-18|$ (there are no ties since the midpoint $12.5$ is not an integer). That is $b^*\le12$. So the $13$ writers with ideals $0,\dots,12$ vote for Erick and the $8$ writers with ideals $13,\dots,20$ vote for Vicktor. Erick's proposal wins $13$ to $8$.

**Answer: Erick 13, Vicktor 8; Erick wins**

smt-2024-power-12.title: Split by the rival
smt-2024-power-12.body: Let the other proposal be $p\ne10$. If $p\le9$, every writer with ideal $b^*\ge10$ is strictly closer to $10$ than to $p$ (or, if tied, prefers the higher number, which is $10$), so these $11$ writers vote for $10$: a majority of $21$. If $p\ge11$, every writer with ideal $b^*\le10$ is strictly closer to $10$ than to $p$ (a tie can only occur at $b^*=\frac{10+p}{2}>10$), so these $11$ writers vote for $10$. Either way $10$ gets at least $11$ votes. ∎

smt-2024-power-13.title: Proof
smt-2024-power-13.body: Let $a$ be the proposal the median writer prefers, $b$ the other one, and $m$ the median ideal. $m\ne b$ (otherwise the median would prefer $b$). *Case $m>b$.* Then $a>b$: if $a<b<m$ then $a$ is farther from $m$ than $b$, contradicting the median's preference. Also $|a-m|\le|b-m|=m-b$. For any writer with ideal $q\ge m$: $$|q-a|\le|q-m|+|m-a|\le(q-m)+(m-b)=q-b=|q-b|,$$ so $q$ is at least as close to $a$ as to $b$; in case of a tie the writer prefers the higher number, which is $a$. So all writers with ideal $\ge m$ (a majority, as $m$ is the median) vote for $a$. *Case $m<b$.* Since the median prefers $a$ and ties go to the higher number, we must have $|a-m|<|b-m|=b-m$. For any writer with ideal $q\le m$: $$|q-a|\le(m-q)+|a-m|<(m-q)+(b-m)=b-q=|q-b|,$$ so they strictly prefer $a$. Again a majority votes for $a$. ∎

smt-2024-power-14.title: Example
smt-2024-power-14.body: Take seven writers: two with ideal $1$, two with ideal $2$, three with ideal $3$, and the three outcomes $1,2,3$. Each writer votes for the outcome equal to their ideal, so outcome $3$ gets $3$ votes and outcomes $1$, $2$ get $2$ each: outcome $3$ wins. But the median ideal (the 4th of $1,1,2,2,3,3,3$) is $2$, so the median writer's favorite outcome is $2$. (Any valid example works.)

smt-2024-power-15.title: Split the vote
smt-2024-power-15.body:
Yes. Suppose Isaack suggests $15$. Writers with ideals $0$ to $8$ vote for Erick ($9$ votes), those with ideals $9$ to $12$ vote for Vicktor ($4$ votes), and those with ideals $13$ to $20$ vote for Isaack ($8$ votes). Erick gets the most votes, $9$ vs $4$ vs $8$. (The values $15$ through $20$ all work; a computer check shows no value below $15$ does.)

**Answer: e.g. 15 bobas**

smt-2024-power-16.title: Erick is always squeezed
smt-2024-power-16.body:
No writer with ideal below $15$ will ever vote for Erick, since Vicktor's $14$ is always at least as close for ideals $\le14$ (for ideal exactly $14.5$ there is none; ties go higher but integer ideals $\le14$ are strictly closer to $14$). So Erick's best case is the writers with ideals $15$ to $20$: at most $6$ votes. Then Vicktor and Isaack split the remaining $15$ votes, so one of them gets at least $8>6$. Hence Erick can never win.

**Answer: No**

smt-2024-power-17.title: Check the process
smt-2024-power-17.body:
$x$ beats $y$ (Alice, Bob) and $y$ beats $z$ (Alice, Carl). Order $z,y,x$: $z$ starts; $y$ beats $z$ and becomes standing best; $x$ beats $y$ and becomes standing best: final outcome $x$. The ordering $y,z,x$ also works: $y$ beats $z$, then $x$ beats $y$.

**Answer: $z,y,x$**

smt-2024-power-18.title: Check the process
smt-2024-power-18.body:
$y$ beats $z$ (Alice, Carl) and $z$ beats $x$ (Bob, Carl). Order $x,z,y$: $x$ starts; $z$ beats $x$; $y$ beats $z$: final outcome $y$. The ordering $z,x,y$ also works.

**Answer: $x,z,y$**

smt-2024-power-19.title: Proof
smt-2024-power-19.body:
($\Rightarrow$) Let $x$ be a Condorcet winner. When $x$'s turn comes (or at the start if it is first), $x$ beats the standing best (more individuals prefer $x$ to any other outcome), so $x$ becomes the standing best, and thereafter no outcome beats it, so it stays standing best to the end. So every ordering yields $x$.

($\Leftarrow$) Suppose there is no Condorcet winner, and let $y$ be the outcome selected for some ordering. Since $y$ is not a Condorcet winner, some outcome $z$ is preferred to $y$ by more individuals. Consider an ordering starting with $y$, then $z$, then the rest arbitrarily. $y$ starts as standing best, and $z$ replaces it. Each outcome is considered only once, in order, so $y$ can never become the standing best again; hence this ordering gives a different outcome than $y$, and not all orderings lead to the same outcome. By contraposition, if all orderings lead to the same outcome there is a Condorcet winner. ∎

smt-2024-power-20a.title: Counterexample
smt-2024-power-20a.body: If there are two outcomes $a,b$ such that neither is unanimously better than the other (e.g. two individuals with $a\succ_1b$ and $b\succ_2a$), then neither $a\succ b$ nor $b\succ a$ holds, so the output is not complete. ∎

smt-2024-power-20b.title: Proof
smt-2024-power-20b.body: Suppose $a\succ b$ and $b\succ c$. Then every individual has $a\succ_ib$ and $b\succ_ic$, so by transitivity of each $\succ_i$, $a\succ_ic$ for all $i$. Hence $a\succ c$. ∎

smt-2024-power-20c.title: Proof
smt-2024-power-20c.body: If $a\succ_ib$ for all $i$, then $a$ is unanimously preferred to $b$, so $a\succ b$ by definition. ∎

smt-2024-power-20d.title: Proof
smt-2024-power-20d.body: Suppose $\{i:a\succ_ib\}=\{i:x\succ_iy\}=I'$. If $I'=I$ (everyone), then $a\succ b$ and $x\succ y$ both hold. If $I'\ne I$, then neither $a\succ b$ nor $x\succ y$ holds. So $a\succ b\iff x\succ y$. ∎

smt-2024-power-20e.title: Proof
smt-2024-power-20e.body: If the output is not complete (as in part (a)), it cannot equal any individual's complete preference order, so there is no dictator in that case. ∎

smt-2024-power-21a.title: Proof
smt-2024-power-21a.body: For any $a\ne b$, the scores $s(a),s(b)$ are numbers that are not equal (no ties), so either $s(a)<s(b)$ or $s(b)<s(a)$, i.e. $a\succ b$ or $b\succ a$. ∎

smt-2024-power-21b.title: Proof
smt-2024-power-21b.body: If $a\succ b$ and $b\succ c$ then $s(a)<s(b)$ and $s(b)<s(c)$, so $s(a)<s(c)$, i.e. $a\succ c$. ∎

smt-2024-power-21c.title: Proof
smt-2024-power-21c.body: Suppose $a\succ_ib$ for all $i$. For each $i$, every outcome better than $a$ is also better than $b$, and $a$ itself is better than $b$ but not better than $a$; so $a_i<b_i$. Summing, $s(a)<s(b)$, hence $a\succ b$. ∎

smt-2024-power-21d.title: Counterexample
smt-2024-power-21d.body: Take two individuals and outcomes $a,b,c,x,y,z$ with $a\succ_1b\succ_1x\succ_1c\succ_1y\succ_1z$ and $c\succ_2b\succ_2x\succ_2y\succ_2z\succ_2a$. Then $s(a)=0+5=5$, $s(b)=1+1=2$, $s(c)=3+0=3$, so $b\succ c$ and $b\succ a$. But $\{i:a\succ_ib\}=\{1\}=\{i:b\succ_ic\}$, so neutrality would require $a\succ b\iff b\succ c$; here $b\succ c$ holds but $a\succ b$ does not. So Borda Count is not neutral. ∎

smt-2024-power-21e.title: Counterexample
smt-2024-power-21e.body: Take two individuals and outcomes $a,b,c$ with $a\succ_1b\succ_1c$ and $c\succ_2a\succ_2b$. Then $s(a)=0+1=1$, $s(b)=1+2=3$, $s(c)=2+0=2$, so Borda Count outputs $a\succ c\succ b$, which equals neither individual's preferences. ∎

smt-2024-power-22.title: Both directions
smt-2024-power-22.body: ($\Leftarrow$) If $\succ=\succ_1$ (the one individual is a dictator) and $a\succ_ib$ for all $i$ (just $i=1$), then $a\succ b$: efficient. ($\Rightarrow$) Suppose the function is efficient. If $a\succ_1b$ then since $1$ is the only individual, efficiency gives $a\succ b$. So for every pair, the aggregated order agrees with $\succ_1$. Since both are strict complete orders, $\succ=\succ_1$, i.e. individual $1$ is a dictator. ∎

smt-2024-power-23.title: Proof
smt-2024-power-23.body: By sufficient diversity there are outcomes $a,b$ with some individuals having $a\succ_ib$ and others $b\succ_ia$; with two individuals this means one prefers $a$ to $b$ and the other prefers $b$ to $a$. The aggregated preferences are complete and strict, so the function outputs either $a\succ b$ or $b\succ a$. In the first case take $x=a$, $y=b$; in the second take $x=b$, $y=a$. In both cases one individual prefers $x$ to $y$, the other prefers $y$ to $x$, and the function outputs $x\succ y$. ∎

smt-2024-power-24.title: Proof
smt-2024-power-24.body: Take outcomes $a,b$ with $a\succ_1b$. If also $a\succ_2b$ then efficiency gives $a\succ b$. If $b\succ_2a$, then $\{i:a\succ_ib\}=\{1\}=\{i:x\succ_iy\}$, so by neutrality $a\succ b$ iff $x\succ y$, and $x\succ y$ holds. Hence $a\succ b$. ∎

smt-2024-power-25.title: Proof
smt-2024-power-25.body: By the previous problem, whenever $a\succ_1b$ the function outputs $a\succ b$, for every pair of outcomes $a,b$. Since both $\succ$ and $\succ_1$ are strict complete orders, $\succ=\succ_1$. So individual $1$ is a dictator. ∎

smt-2024-power-26.title: Proof
smt-2024-power-26.body: By Problem 4.4 there exist outcomes $x,y$ such that one individual prefers $x$ to $y$, the other prefers $y$ to $x$, and the function outputs $x\succ y$. Call the individual who prefers $x$ to $y$ individual $1$. Then the hypotheses of Problem 4.6 hold, so individual $1$ is a dictator. ∎
